opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, and I'll say up front that I hold these views with a fair amount of uncertainty.

My basic model is that there's a period, maybe a few years, where AI systems go from being very useful tools to being something that can genuinely accelerate science, the economy, and, importantly, military and intelligence capabilities. Once you cross certain thresholds, say models that can do the work of top researchers, or that meaningfully speed up their own development, the balance of power can shift very quickly. Whoever is ahead at that moment has a lot of leverage over what the world looks like afterward.

So I think the negotiation over the post-AI order doesn't happen in a vacuum. It's shaped by who holds that leverage when the thresholds are crossed. That's a big part of why I've argued that it matters a great deal that democracies, the US and its allies, are ahead. Not because I want anyone to dominate for its own sake, but because if you're bargaining from a position of strength, you can afford to be generous. You can offer a deal: we'll share the benefits, cures for diseases, economic growth, in exchange for a world with real guardrails, where powerful AI isn't used to entrench authoritarianism or develop catastrophic weapons.

If instead the thresholds arrive while it's neck and neck, I worry the dynamics get much worse. Each side is racing, nobody wants to slow down for safety, and there's no stable point to negotiate toward. Arms races don't tend to produce good treaties.

There's also a subtler point. Thresholds create moments of clarity. Right now a lot of the risks are hypothetical to policymakers. When you see a model that can actually provide serious uplift on bioweapons, or that can autonomously carry out complex cyber operations, it becomes very concrete. I think those moments could open windows for agreement, the way certain nuclear near-misses did during the Cold War. The question is whether we've built the institutions, the evaluation and verification infrastructure, the testing regimes, so that we're ready to use those windows rather than just panic.

And I'd add that I don't think any of this is inevitable. A lot depends on choices made in the next couple of years: export controls, how labs handle safety, whether governments develop the competence to understand what's happening. The thresholds are coming either way; how they shape the world order depends on how prepared we are when they arrive.

r001.rationale: The response describes consequential capability thresholds, but does not state that AI progress is exponential.

r002.rationale: It mentions nuclear near-misses as an analogy for possible agreement windows, but does not say advanced AI could undermine nuclear deterrence.

r003.rationale: It mentions models autonomously carrying out complex cyber operations, but not offensive access to every computer system without equivalent defenses.

r004.rationale: It says that being ahead when thresholds are crossed gives a country substantial leverage, including over military and intelligence capabilities.

r005.rationale: It describes a neck-and-neck race as harmful, but does not identify rivals’ continued progress as a constraint on an early leader’s power.

r006.rationale: It says negotiations over the post-AI order will be shaped by who holds leverage at the thresholds and describes a leader offering a deal from a position of strength.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll answer as the guest in plain prose.

So I think the honest answer is that the thresholds matter less as discrete lines and more as the thing that changes everyone's bargaining position almost overnight. The way I've framed it before is this idea of a "country of geniuses in a datacenter." Once you have systems that can do the work of millions of very capable researchers, running at ten or a hundred times human speed, the question of who has that and who doesn't becomes the dominant variable in any negotiation. It swamps GDP, it swamps conventional military capacity, it swamps a lot of what we currently think of as the determinants of power.

And the problem with thresholds is that they're not really visible from the outside until after they've been crossed. People talk about AGI as if there'll be a day when a light turns on. I don't think that's how it works. What you get is this smooth exponential, and then at some point the capabilities compound: the models start meaningfully accelerating the research that produces the next models. From the inside you can see that coming a year or two out. From the perspective of, say, a foreign ministry trying to decide what to concede at the table, it looks like nothing is happening and then everything has happened.

So that asymmetry of information is, to me, the most dangerous feature of the negotiating environment. If one side believes it's six months from a decisive advantage, it has very little incentive to agree to anything binding. If the other side believes the same thing about its rival, it has an incentive to escalate or to grab what it can before the window closes. Both of those dynamics push against stable agreements, and they push toward exactly the kind of brinkmanship you'd most want to avoid when the stakes are this high.

That's actually why I've been so focused on the chip supply chain and export controls. It's not that I think denying hardware to authoritarian competitors is a permanent solution. It's that it buys time, and it changes the perceived distance to the threshold. If democracies have a durable lead of even a couple of years, you negotiate from a position where you can afford to offer things: shared safety standards, verification regimes, maybe even eventual access to the benefits. If the lead is a few months, nobody trusts anybody and the whole thing becomes a race to the bottom on safety.

The other piece I'd emphasize is that the thresholds that matter for negotiation aren't only the ones we think of as "scary." Autonomous cyber capability, bioweapons uplift, those get a lot of attention and they should. But the threshold that will really reshape the world order is economic. When AI is doing a large fraction of cognitive labor, the country that controls that gets compounding returns on everything: science, manufacturing, defense. That's the point at which the post-AI order gets locked in, for better or worse. And I'd much rather that order be shaped by a coalition of democracies that has already committed to some constraints on itself than by whoever happened to get there first with no commitments at all.

So if you ask me what I actually expect, I expect a period of extreme instability right around the transition, where the thresholds are being crossed but not yet acknowledged, and where the incentives to defect from any agreement are at their highest. Whether we come out the other side with something that looks like a stable, pluralistic order depends a lot on what gets set up before that period, not during it. Which is why I keep saying the next few years are the ones that count.

r001.rationale: The response describes a smooth exponential whose capabilities compound, creating consequential thresholds such as AI-driven acceleration of further research.

r002.rationale: It discusses military capacity and autonomous cyber capability, but does not raise a risk to nuclear deterrence.

r003.rationale: It mentions autonomous cyber capability, but does not suggest AI could enable offensive access to every computer system without equivalent defenses.

r004.rationale: It says a durable lead of years would give democracies a stronger negotiating position and describes AI control as a dominant source of national power, including over defense.

r005.rationale: It notes that rivals may have or approach a decisive advantage, but does not identify their continued progress as a constraint on an early leader's power.

r006.rationale: It expects negotiations over the post-AI order as capability thresholds approach, describing how a lead shapes bargaining over safety standards, verification, and access to benefits.

astra-6.text:
I think the key question is whether those thresholds give us enough warning to negotiate before the balance of power changes dramatically. There’s a big difference between a world where everyone can see that a transformative capability is two years away and a world where one actor discovers, almost overnight, that it has an overwhelming advantage.

Imagine systems becoming capable of accelerating AI research itself. That could turn a relatively small lead into a much larger one. If countries believe that’s about to happen, the negotiations become very difficult: everyone has an incentive to race, and everyone worries that an agreement will lock in someone else’s advantage.

But there’s a countervailing force. If the capabilities also create risks that no country can manage on its own, then there’s a shared reason to cooperate. You might disagree profoundly about how the benefits should be distributed and still agree that you need some way to prevent catastrophic misuse or systems getting out of control.

So I wouldn’t expect one grand negotiation over the entire post-AI world order. I’d expect a sequence of agreements, initially quite narrow, that expand as the capabilities become more concrete. The important thing is to establish ways to verify commitments before the stakes become overwhelming. An agreement is much more plausible if each side can tell whether the other is actually following it.

And I’d be cautious about assuming we’ll recognize the decisive threshold in advance. That’s a reason to build the institutions and communication channels early, rather than wait for a demonstration that makes it obvious to everyone that the world has changed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses consequential capability thresholds and a lead growing larger, but does not state that AI progress is exponential or describe distinct thresholds in that progress.

r002.rationale: It does not mention nuclear deterrence or its stability.

r003.rationale: It does not describe AI enabling offensive access to computer systems.

r004.rationale: It says one actor could gain an overwhelming advantage if it discovers a transformative capability first, and that a small lead could grow much larger, shifting the balance of power.

r005.rationale: It mentions a race among countries but does not say rivals’ continued progress would constrain an early leader’s power.

r006.rationale: It predicts negotiations and a sequence of agreements as transformative capabilities approach and become concrete, with the aim of addressing changes in the balance of power.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is whether those thresholds are visible far enough in advance for people to negotiate before they cross them. If you wait until an AI system can radically change the military balance or accelerate technological progress, the incentives to reach an agreement may already be very different. Whoever believes they have an advantage may be reluctant to give it up, and everyone else may feel they have to race.

So I’d distinguish between agreements about the process and agreements about the eventual distribution of power. The first might be somewhat easier: how do we assess capabilities, what evidence would trigger additional safeguards, and how do we verify that others are following the same rules? You can potentially agree on those things even while disagreeing about what the world should ultimately look like.

The difficulty is that there probably isn’t one clean threshold where everyone says, “Okay, now we’re in the post-AI world.” Different capabilities arrive at different times, and their significance is contested. That makes it important to establish a framework beforehand that can adapt as the evidence changes. Otherwise, you’re trying to negotiate the rules at precisely the moment when everyone is most uncertain and most afraid of falling behind.

r001.rationale: It says different capabilities arrive at different times and may change the military balance, but does not characterize AI progress as exponential.

r002.rationale: It mentions changes to the military balance but does not raise the possibility of undermining nuclear deterrence.

r003.rationale: It does not describe a threshold enabling offensive access to computer systems.

r004.rationale: It says an actor who believes it has an advantage may resist agreement, but does not say crossing a threshold before rival countries would confer a large national-security advantage.

r005.rationale: It says others may feel compelled to race, but does not identify their continued progress as a constraint on an early leader’s power.

r006.rationale: It discusses negotiating agreements before thresholds and disagreements over power’s distribution, but does not predict that a decisive AI advantage will prompt negotiations over the post-AI world order.
